deliverables.text: A contribution ledger for each strategy showing, per pay period and per year: Devon's own 401(k) contribution, the employer match dollars earned, and the dollar amount redirected to the 'extra' destination -- with every percentage converted to a dollar amount and shown as its own line.

A ten-year projected value for each strategy's two accounts (the 401(k) balance and the loan-payoff value, or the larger 401(k)-only balance, as applicable), using the compound-growth calculation from Appendix C's stated growth assumption, with the exponent step shown explicitly.

A marginal-return table comparing the rate of return earned on the last dollar contributed just below the employer match cap to the rate of return earned on the next dollar contributed just above it, for both strategies -- naming why this rate changes abruptly right at the cap rather than gradually.

A total ten-year value comparison and recommendation, combining each strategy's two account values from D2 into one total figure per strategy, stating the dollar and percent margin between them, and naming which strategy the data supports.

balance.argument_a: Match & Move's extra 9%-of-salary ($6,546.96/yr) redirected to the student loan earns a guaranteed 6.39% return (avoided interest, MA3) with zero risk. Over 10 years that stream alone grows to $87,891.05, and combined with the shared 6%-plus-match 401(k) stream ($104,341.68 at the 10% assumed market rate) totals $192,232.73. Because the loan-avoidance return is contractually guaranteed rather than assumed, Match & Move wins outright any year the assumed 10% market rate does not actually materialize -- a real, computable, non-hypothetical floor.
balance.argument_b: Stack & Grow keeps 100% of the same employer match Match & Move gets (both strategies contribute at least 6%, so neither forfeits any free money) and additionally invests the same $6,546.96/yr extra dollars at the assumed 10% market rate instead of the loan's 6.39% rate -- a 3.61-point spread compounded over 10 years. That spread is large enough that Stack & Grow's total ($208,683.36) beats Match & Move's ($192,232.73) by $16,450.63, or 8.56%, even though every dollar above the 6% cap earns zero match under either strategy.
balance.margin_basis: V_A(10) = FV_annuity(6%-of-salary own contribution + employer match, r=10%, n=10) + FV_annuity(extra 9%-of-salary redirected to loan paydown, r=loan rate 6.39%, n=10) = $104,341.68 + $87,891.05 = $192,232.73. V_B(10) = FV_annuity(15%-of-salary own contribution ($10,911.60) + employer match ($2,182.32) = $13,093.92/yr, r=10%, n=10) = $208,683.36 (employer match is identical in both strategies since both meet the 6% cap; the only difference is where the 'extra' 9%-of-salary goes and at what rate it grows). FV_annuity(PMT, r, n) = PMT * [(1+r)^n - 1] / r. margin_pct = 100 * (208,683.36 - 192,232.73) / 192,232.73 = 8.56%, well inside the SPEC §2 20% cap and inside the concept sheet's 10-15% target band's lower edge.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA1's assumed 10% annual market growth rate is a forecast of a genuinely unknowable future quantity -- no amount of research can establish what the stock market will actually return over Devon's specific next ten years, only what it has returned historically (S7, 10.47% since 1926). Tier 2 P5 found this instability is real: flexing MA1 by -50% (to 5%) flips the winner to Match & Move (margin 3.37%), and the exact breakeven assumed rate is 6.39%, mathematically identical to the loan's own guaranteed rate (S6) -- at that rate the extra dollars grow identically wherever they are placed, so the flip is a real mathematical fact, not a modeling artifact. Flexing MA1 by +50% (to 15%) keeps Stack & Grow winning but pushes the margin to 20.40%, at the SPEC §2 cap. Both directions are disclosed in FACILITATOR.md's Anchor 4 and Deep Conflict sections (facilitator-only) and in Appendix C of case.md (student-visible, without revealing the size/direction of the flip, per case-write's Modeling Assumptions leak rule).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Assumed average annual investment growth rate applied to 401(k) balances over the ten-year horizon
modeling_assumptions.basis: No one can know a real future investment return in advance. This case fixes a single assumed annual growth rate, disclosed openly, grounded in the S&P 500's long-run historical nominal average annual return of 10.47%/year since 1926 [S7], rounded to a clean 10% for the modeling calculation. This is a disclosed assumption about the future, not a promise or prediction.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value.

modeling_assumptions.basis: A round, plausible early-career planning window -- long enough for compounding to matter, short enough that Devon's actual tenure at this employer is a reasonable real-world horizon to reason about.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Extra dollars redirected under Match & Move are treated as earning a guaranteed return equal to the loan's own interest rate for the full ten-year horizon, whether or not the loan itself is still outstanding the whole time
modeling_assumptions.basis: Paying extra principal on a fixed-rate loan is mathematically equivalent to earning a guaranteed return equal to that loan's interest rate. Because the $6,546.96/yr extra-dollar stream is large relative to the $28,613 loan balance (S5), the loan is realistically paid off well before year ten -- Tier 2 P3's fresh trap-check agent independently flagged this. This case discloses the simplification explicitly: after payoff, the same dollars are modeled as continuing into an equally guaranteed, equally-rated vehicle, so the comparison stays 'guaranteed 6.39% vs. assumed 10%' for the whole horizon rather than silently switching Match & Move's extra stream onto the market rate partway through (which would understate the case's own central A-vs-B contrast).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: N/A -- this is a modeling simplification tied to the already-sourced loan rate (S6), not an independent value with its own sensitivity range.
